issues.description: The methods state that all included studies collected the CREP-specified minimum sample size of 120, but the immediately preceding and tabulated sample sizes show that most included studies had fewer than 120 participants. This contradiction affects assessment of study eligibility, power, and adherence to preregistered/CREP criteria.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

issues.description: The reported range of sample sizes includes values well below the stated minimum of 120, and Table 1 lists multiple studies with N = 80, 81, 90, 94, and 116. This raises concerns about whether inclusion criteria were consistently applied and whether some studies were underpowered relative to the stated design.
issues.quote: Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374.

issues.subcategory: incorrect use of metafor rma inputs
issues.description: The manuscript says the metafor rma function was supplied with effect size r and N parameters. The rma() function requires effect-size estimates and corresponding sampling variances/standard errors, not merely r and N unless transformed/processed appropriately. Correlations should typically be Fisher z-transformed and analyzed with correct sampling variances, then back-transformed. If raw r values were meta-analyzed directly with N as variance or an unsupported argument, estimates, standard errors, CIs, p-values, heterogeneity, and prediction intervals may be wrong.
issues.quote: The rma function was used, which accepts the effect size r and N parameters

issues.subcategory: correlation meta-analysis without Fisher z transformation
issues.description: The manuscript reports meta-analyzing effect size r directly, with no indication that correlations were Fisher z-transformed before synthesis. Meta-analysis of raw correlations can yield biased CIs and improper weighting because the sampling variance of r depends on the true correlation. This matters especially for inference, prediction intervals, and heterogeneity estimates.
issues.quote: we chose to calculate effect size r for all four outcome variables in the study. The replication effect size r statistics were calculated in the same way for consistency.

issues.subcategory: incorrect equivalence of beta and correlation
issues.description: The note states that standardized beta is equivalent to effect size r. This is only true in a simple bivariate regression with one predictor and no covariates, and only under standard conditions. The manuscript does not clearly establish that all original and replication regressions were identical simple regressions without additional predictors. If not, treating beta as r would be incorrect and would distort the meta-analysis and comparisons.
issues.quote: Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.description: Table 3 appears to compute 'Difference' inconsistently. For example, replication r = -0.02 and original r = -0.33 would yield replication minus original = +0.31, not -0.31; original minus replication would be -0.31. But for other rows such as Gordon express, replication r = -0.10 and original r = 0.15 would yield replication minus original = -0.25 or original minus replication = 0.25. The sign convention is inconsistent across sections/outcomes. This affects interpretation of whether replications were larger or smaller than the original.

issues.subcategory: text conflicts with table on effect-size comparisons
issues.description: The text says six of seven self-disclosure advantage comparisons were not significantly different from the original, but Table 3 shows BYU-Sp16 has a CI excluding zero. Because of the apparent sign errors and ambiguous difference definition, conclusions about which replications differ from the original are unreliable.
issues.quote: the effect size differences comparing six of the seven replications to the original were not significantly different from zero

issues.subcategory: incorrect prediction interval reported as confidence interval
issues.description: The manuscript states that a 95% confidence interval and prediction interval indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14. A confidence interval does not indicate where future study effects will fall; that is the role of a prediction interval. Conflating CIs and PIs misstates uncertainty and can overstate replicability.
issues.quote: the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14

issues.description: The discussion repeatedly interprets prediction intervals as showing that 95% of future studies would find effects within the interval. Prediction intervals estimate the distribution of true effects in comparable settings under model assumptions, not guaranteed observed effects in future studies. With only seven studies, PI estimates are especially uncertain. This overstates precision and predictive certainty.
issues.quote: the PI [.01, .14] showed that 95% of future studies would find an effect size smaller than the original study’s

issues.description: The prediction interval for self-disclosure safety is reported differently in the Results and Discussion. Results give 95% PI [-.54, -.03], whereas Discussion reports 95% PI [-.40, -.15]. This numerical inconsistency affects the claimed robustness of the effect.

The prediction interval for opportunity to connect is reported differently in the Results and Discussion. Results report 95% PI [-.09, .26], while Discussion reports 95% PI [-.07, .27]. Although small, this indicates calculation or reporting inconsistency.

The fail-safe number for opportunity to express self is reported as 3 studies in the Results but 5 studies in the Discussion. This discrepancy undermines confidence in the calculations and interpretation of robustness.
issues.quote: The FSN was 3 studies.

issues.description: The fail-safe number for opportunity to connect is reported as 5 studies in the Results but 11 studies in the Discussion. This materially changes the conclusion about stability of the finding.
issues.quote: The FSN was 5 studies.

issues.subcategory: fail-safe number used when meta-analytic effect nonsignificant
issues.description: Fail-safe N is described as identifying how many nonsignificant unpublished studies would reduce a significant meta-analytic result to nonsignificance, yet it is reported for the opportunity-to-connect outcome where the meta-analytic result is nonsignificant (p = .065). This is conceptually inappropriate or at least uninterpretable under the authors' own stated definition.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065. ... The FSN was 5 studies.

issues.subcategory: fail-safe number used to infer absence of effect
issues.description: The manuscript uses a small fail-safe N to support confidence in 'lack of an effect' for expression, even though the meta-analytic effect is statistically significant (p = .021) and FSN is designed around robustness of significant effects to unpublished null studies, not evidence for a null effect. This reverses the logic of the statistic and may mislead readers.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.

issues.subcategory: contradictory inference from significant meta-analysis and null conclusion
issues.description: For opportunity to express self, the meta-analysis reports r = .08, p = .021 and a PI not including zero, but the manuscript frames the result as supporting no relation. A statistically significant pooled effect is not equivalent to no effect simply because individual studies were nonsignificant. The appropriate conclusion would be a small positive association with uncertainty, or the need for equivalence testing if claiming absence.
issues.quote: Even though the effect size meta-analysis revealed that the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero... all individual replications found regression coefficients not significantly different from zero.

issues.subcategory: lack of equivalence/noninferiority testing for null claims
issues.description: The manuscript concludes that self-esteem does not relate to expression and provides no evidence for connection, but it did not conduct equivalence tests or specify smallest effect sizes of interest. Nonsignificant individual coefficients and CIs including zero do not establish absence of effect. This is especially important because the pooled expression effect is statistically significant.
issues.quote: self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression

issues.description: The authors cite p-values between .04 and .05 as more likely under the true null than false one and use this to cast doubt on the original p = .05. This is an oversimplified and potentially misleading interpretation; the evidential value of a p-value depends on power, priors, and analysis context. A single p-value at .05 is weak evidence, but the stated rationale is not a valid general inference.
issues.quote: p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one

issues.subcategory: publication bias inferred from replication-original difference
issues.description: The discussion interprets smaller replication effects and a PI below the original as indicating publication bias in the original study. Smaller replication effects can arise from sampling error, contextual change, measurement differences, implementation differences, or regression to the mean. Publication bias cannot be inferred from a single original study compared with seven replications without appropriate bias models or a corpus of original studies.
issues.quote: all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study

issues.description: The original study did not specify whether the questionnaires were administered in lab or online, so replication teams used different modes. Mode of administration can affect self-disclosure and social desirability responses, particularly for online/Facebook-related constructs. This variation weakens claims that all studies were direct replications and may introduce unexplored heterogeneity.
issues.quote: researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods)

issues.description: One replication administered questionnaires in groups of two to six, whereas other studies had participants complete alone or online. Group settings may alter privacy perceptions, self-esteem responding, or Facebook self-disclosure attitudes, directly relevant to the constructs measured. This procedural variation is not controlled analytically.
issues.quote: Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.description: One study altered item order and wording on four Rosenberg self-esteem items, including removing 'At times' from an item. Such changes can affect item severity and scale scores, threatening measurement equivalence across replication sites and with the original.
issues.quote: one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., ‘At times I think I am no good at all’ vs. ‘I think I am no good at all’)

issues.description: Two replications used a five-point Rosenberg self-esteem scale whereas most used the original four-point scale. Changing response options can alter means, variances, reliability, and regression coefficients. Although standardized coefficients reduce some scale metric issues, response format may still affect construct measurement and comparability.
issues.quote: most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges several methodological differences but does not model or otherwise assess their impact, partly because there are too few studies. These differences may confound site effects with true replication effects and limit interpretation of pooled estimates.
issues.quote: we know there are methodological and procedural differences between the studies (i.e., in-person vs. online; individual participants vs. groups; wording on questionnaires; additional measures). Because each of these potential moderating factors occurred in only one or two of the seven replications, we chose not to explore these issues in more depth.

issues.subcategory: perceived affordances versus actual Facebook behavior
issues.description: The outcomes measure participants' perceptions that Facebook provides expression, connection, safety, and advantages, not actual self-disclosure, expression, connection, benefits, or social outcomes. Some discussion claims move toward actual behavior and benefits, which are not directly measured.
issues.quote: participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers

issues.description: The discussion invokes a benefits-risk analysis framework and claims the present research supports it, but the study did not measure perceived risks and benefits as a decision process, actual disclosure decisions, or social support outcomes. The data are limited to cross-sectional self-reports of perceived Facebook advantages/safety.
issues.quote: When choosing what information to self-disclose, people engage in a benefits-risk analysis... This perspective is supported by the present research.

issues.subcategory: Facebook comparison may be outdated or ambiguous
issues.description: Participants in 2016-2017 may interpret Facebook differently from participants in the original 2012 study, particularly given shifts to Instagram/Snapchat. The manuscript later acknowledges implicit platform comparisons, but this threatens construct equivalence of 'Facebook opportunities' across time and sites.
issues.quote: Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram when rating its usefulness for self-expression and connection with others

issues.description: The study uses cross-sectional regression of self-esteem predicting perceptions. While regression terminology often says 'predictor,' the discussion sometimes implies that low self-esteem causes perceptions of Facebook as safer/advantageous. Without experimental manipulation or longitudinal design, causal direction and confounding cannot be established.
issues.quote: low self-esteem predicts perceptions that Facebook is a safer and more advantageous place to self-disclose than FTF interactions

issues.description: Associations between self-esteem and Facebook perceptions may be confounded by variables such as social anxiety, depression, extraversion, Facebook use intensity, prior negative face-to-face experiences, or platform preference. No covariates or design controls are reported, limiting interpretation of self-esteem as the relevant explanatory factor.
issues.quote: self-esteem as a predictor of Facebook users’ perceptions of the site’s usefulness for self-expression, self-disclosure, and connection with others

issues.description: Although the manuscript claims preregistration, it does not summarize key preregistered hypotheses, exclusion rules, missing data procedures, planned analyses, deviations, or whether the meta-analysis itself was preregistered. Readers must consult multiple OSF pages, limiting transparency and replicability from the manuscript.
issues.quote: the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study’s OSF page

issues.description: The authors compared REML and DerSimonian-Laird and selected REML because it produced 'more interpretable' heterogeneity estimates. Unless this choice was preregistered, selecting an estimator after inspecting results is an analytic degree of freedom. 'More interpretable' is subjective and insufficiently specified.
issues.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data

issues.subcategory: unclear inclusion criteria for OSF forks
issues.description: There were 17 forks but only seven studies included. The manuscript says included studies met minimum sample size and posted data/results, but given the contradiction about minimum sample size, criteria are unclear. It is not reported whether excluded forks had data, incomplete data, failed review, or other reasons. Selective inclusion could bias the meta-analysis.
issues.quote: The Forest and Wood (2012) CREP replication project page on the OSF has 17 “forks”... These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that missing data handling could not always be determined. Missing responses on multi-item scales or outcome variables can affect sample sizes, reliability, means, correlations, and regression estimates. Without clear handling rules, replication and bias assessment are limited.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.description: There is no systematic reporting of participant exclusions, incomplete responses, or item-level missingness across sites. Since sample sizes differ from stated targets and some datasets lacked item-level data, it is impossible to evaluate attrition/missing data bias or whether analyses used complete-case, pairwise, imputation, or other procedures.
issues.quote: Data were not always collected or stored consistently... individual item-level data were not always stored

issues.description: The manuscript states that most studies appeared to mean-average items, while the Gordon study appeared to sum items. Although standardization may mitigate scale metric issues in regressions, inconsistent composite creation affects descriptive statistics and potentially analyses if not standardized before regression. The lack of clear scoring procedures compromises reproducibility.
issues.quote: The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study’s mean implied items were summed.

issues.description: Race data were collected in only three replications and other demographic variables were generally not collected. This limits evaluation of sample comparability, site differences, and generalizability. The rationale that the original did not collect such information is insufficient for a multi-site replication intended to assess generalizability.
issues.quote: In three replications (BYU-Wi17, IIT-Sp16, and IIT-Sp17), race data was collected, but in all other studies no other demographic information was collected

issues.description: All participants were undergraduates at five U.S. institutions. The manuscript discusses implications for Facebook users and social compensation theory broadly, but the sample is limited in age, education, country, and likely Facebook usage patterns. Generalization to the broader Facebook population or two billion users is not warranted without stronger caveats.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US

issues.description: The manuscript describes the institutions as diverse, but all are U.S. colleges/universities and participants are undergraduates. Institutional diversity does not ensure demographic, cultural, age, or nonstudent diversity. This framing may overstate generalizability.
issues.quote: These CREP research teams represented five diverse institutions, both public and private, in urban and suburban settings in the eastern and western U.S.

issues.subcategory: broad claims about individuals with low self-esteem
issues.description: The conclusion generalizes to 'individuals with low self-esteem' rather than U.S. undergraduate Facebook users in 2016-2017. This overextends the sample and study context.
issues.quote: We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions

issues.subcategory: social compensation theory only partially tested
issues.description: The study tests perceptions of Facebook affordances as a function of self-esteem, not whether low self-esteem individuals actually use Facebook to compensate for face-to-face anxiety, whether anxiety is mitigated online, or whether social outcomes improve. Thus claims that the research supports social compensation theory are only indirect and should be more cautious.
issues.quote: The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory

issues.subcategory: theory predictions not aligned with replicated findings
issues.description: The manuscript notes that social compensation theory might predict lower self-esteem individuals use Facebook for expression and connection, yet the meta-analysis finds weak positive or null associations for those outcomes. The theoretical interpretation therefore requires refinement rather than broad support.
issues.quote: social compensation theory might predict that those with lower self-esteem may use Facebook to express themselves and connect with others... This finding runs contrary to the results of our meta-analysis

issues.subcategory: effect size for original advantage inconsistent
issues.description: The original advantage effect is reported as -.30 in the abstract and Table 1 beta, but -.33 in Table 3 and discussion comparisons. This inconsistency affects effect-size comparison calculations and claims about replication similarity.
issues.quote: meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30

issues.description: The Results report the opportunity-to-connect meta-analytic effect as p = .065, but the Discussion states that the meta-analytic effect was significantly different from zero. This is a direct contradiction affecting the main conclusion.
issues.quote: However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.

issues.description: The discussion reports a narrower safety PI than the Results and uses it to support robustness. This discrepancy changes whether future effects may be close to zero and undermines the stated conclusion that the effect is considerable.
issues.quote: The 95% PI [-.40, -.15] indicated that future studies would be likely to find such an effect as well.

issues.description: The manuscript refers to both Collaborative Replication and Education Project and Collaborative Research and Education Project. Although minor, inconsistent naming can confuse readers and indicates editorial imprecision.
issues.quote: Collaborative Research and Education Project (CREP; Grahe, et al., 2016; https://osf.io/wfc6u/)

issues.subcategory: Table 2 omitted in manuscript text provided
issues.description: The manuscript references Table 2 for demographic and descriptive statistics, but the table contents are not actually provided beyond notes. Without full descriptive statistics, readers cannot evaluate scale distributions, site differences, possible range restriction, or comparability to the original study.
issues.quote: Table 2 shows each study’s descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables.

issues.description: The manuscript does not report whether participants were required to be active Facebook users, how Facebook use was verified, or whether non-users/inactive users were excluded. Perceptions of Facebook self-disclosure and connection may differ substantially by use status, making this critical for construct validity and replication fidelity.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted

issues.subcategory: insufficient original-study procedure details for replication fidelity
issues.description: The authors note that the original did not specify lab versus online administration, but do not detail other fidelity checks, exact materials equivalence, recruitment, compensation, instructions, or timing. For a direct replication meta-analysis, enough detail is needed to evaluate how close the replication was to the original.
issues.quote: As the original research did not specify whether participants completed questionnaires in a lab or online

issues.description: Several individual replications had samples around 80-90, similar to the original and smaller than the stated 120 target. Such samples have limited power to detect small effects like r = .08-.16 and imprecise effect estimates, making study-level significance comparisons uninformative and increasing the risk of false negatives.

The manuscript repeatedly counts how many individual replications were statistically significant. Because the replications differ in sample size and are often underpowered, vote-counting by significance can misrepresent evidence. Meta-analytic effect estimates and CIs should be emphasized over counts of significant studies.
issues.quote: Four of the seven replication studies were consistent with the original study, showing self-esteem to be a significant predictor

issues.subcategory: heterogeneity inference with very few studies
issues.description: The manuscript reports Q, T2, and I2 with CIs for only seven studies and sometimes interprets little/limited evidence of heterogeneity. With k = 7, heterogeneity tests have low power and estimates are unstable; the authors acknowledge this limitation later, but the Results still use these statistics to characterize heterogeneity.
issues.quote: The variance measures showed little evidence of heterogeniety, Q(df = 6) = 5.81, p = 0.445; T2 = 0, 95% CI [0, .03]; I2 = 6.08%, 95% CI [0%, 79.94%].

issues.subcategory: inappropriate precision implied by small-k prediction intervals
issues.description: Prediction intervals are reported for meta-analyses with only seven studies, including cases where tau-squared is estimated as zero. Such intervals can be highly unstable and sensitive to estimator choice, yet they are used to make strong claims about future studies. This overstates precision.
issues.quote: 95% PI [-.24, -.08] indicated that future studies are likely to find such an effect

issues.subcategory: single platform operationalization limits social media construct
issues.description: The study frames conclusions in terms of social networking/social media and social compensation, but all focal items concern Facebook. Facebook-specific affordances, norms, and demographics may not represent social media generally, especially during the 2016-2017 shift to other platforms.
issues.quote: psychological issues related to Facebook

issues.description: Because the data are cross-sectional, perceptions of Facebook could influence self-esteem, both could influence each other, or both could be caused by third variables. Regression language of self-esteem 'predicting' perceptions may be statistically acceptable but should not be interpreted temporally or causally.
issues.quote: self-esteem was a predictor of the perception that Facebook is advantageous for self-disclosure over FTF

issues.description: The manuscript states individual studies were preregistered, but not whether the meta-analysis inclusion criteria, effect-size extraction, estimator selection, handling of deviations, and planned interpretations were preregistered. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom in the synthesis.
issues.quote: This meta-analysis synthesized seven direct pre-registered replications

issues.subcategory: lack of recruitment and compensation details
issues.description: The methods do not report how participants were recruited, whether they received course credit or payment, response rates, or whether sampling differed by site. These details are needed to evaluate selection bias and replicate the studies.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted from February, 2016 to June, 2017

issues.description: Some studies included additional personality measures after primary measures. While placed after focal measures, the manuscript does not specify whether participants knew additional measures were coming, whether consent/instructions differed, or whether the Direct-Plus nature affected recruitment or context. This is probably minor but relevant to fidelity.
issues.quote: Some research teams chose a Direct-Plus replication, and included additional personality-type measures following the primary measures.

issues.subcategory: reported original expression effect unavailable but used in comparisons
issues.description: The original study did not report a beta coefficient for expression, yet Table 3 uses an original r = .15 and compares each replication against it. The manuscript does not explain how this original effect size was derived for expression. Without the derivation, the effect-size comparisons are not reproducible.
issues.quote: * The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable.

issues.subcategory: ambiguous original effect extraction from t statistics
issues.description: The authors state original effect sizes were calculated from t-statistics and degrees of freedom, but do not provide formulas, extracted t/df values, or whether effects came from simple or multiple regression. This is necessary to verify effect-size r calculations and equivalence with standardized betas.
issues.quote: The original Forest and Wood (2012) regression results included t-statistics and degrees of freedom for all variables, so we chose to calculate effect size r

issues.description: The study compares a 2012 Facebook study to 2016-2017 replications, during a period of changing platform demographics and affordances. Although discussed as a possible explanation, this temporal change limits conclusions about replicability versus historical/contextual change and should be treated as a central design limitation.
issues.quote: differences between the original and replication results might be related to variations in social media usage patterns across populations

issues.description: The manuscript presents direct replications as evidence about both robustness and generalizability. However, because all samples are similar undergraduate U.S. samples and procedures vary in uncontrolled ways, failures/successes cannot cleanly distinguish replicability of the original effect from boundary conditions or contextual changes.
issues.quote: The results provided further evidence regarding the original study’s generalizability and robustness.

issues.subcategory: CIs including zero interpreted as no effect without considering power
issues.description: The abstract and results use inclusion of zero in individual 95% CIs to assert lack of relation. Wide CIs from small samples are compatible with meaningful effects in either direction; absence of statistical significance is not evidence of absence without equivalence bounds or adequate precision.
issues.quote: across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero

issues.subcategory: unclear scale anchoring and item content
issues.description: The manuscript reports item counts and response ranges but not the actual items or anchors for the Facebook perception scales. Because these are researcher-created measures central to construct validity, readers need item content or a clear reference to accessible materials to evaluate what was measured.
issues.quote: Three items each assessed the degree to which participants believed Facebook enabled them to express themselves and to connect with others.

issues.description: The discussion calls the self-disclosure safety effect 'considerable' based on r around -.28. In psychological terms this is a small-to-moderate association, and its heterogeneity is substantial in the Results. The description may overstate practical magnitude.
issues.quote: the size of this effect is considerable

issues.subcategory: original connect result framing inconsistent with table
issues.description: The original connect effect is described as a significant finding, but Table 1 reports p = .050 exactly. Depending on rounding and alpha convention, this is borderline and should be described cautiously rather than as clearly significant.
issues.quote: Forest and Wood speculated... Study 1 provided mixed support... those lower in self-esteem saw Facebook as...

issues.description: The manuscript treats p = .050 as significant for the original connection effect. If rounded, the exact value could be above or below .05. The exact p-value should be reported or the result described as marginal/borderline, especially because it is central to replication interpretation.

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding irrelevant but procedural reviewer influence unclear
issues.description: Although this is a questionnaire study where participant blinding may be less relevant, undergraduate teams knew they were conducting replications of a known finding. The manuscript does not report whether analysts were blinded to original hypotheses/results or whether standardized scripts minimized expectancy effects. This is a smaller concern but relevant in multi-team replications.
issues.quote: Potential contributors... informed project leaders of their intention to replicate

issues.description: Two IIT studies and two BYU-related studies appear to be conducted at the same institutions across terms. The manuscript does not report whether participants could overlap across waves or how duplicate participation was prevented. Non-independence would affect meta-analytic assumptions.
issues.quote: IIT-Sp16... IIT-Sp17

issues.subcategory: fixed versus random effects rationale insufficiently tied to direct-replication inference
issues.description: The authors chose random effects due to methodological and population heterogeneity, which is defensible, but then interpret the summary effect as a common expectation for future studies. Given only five institutions and uncontrolled deviations, the distribution of effects may not be well estimated or representative of a meaningful superpopulation.
issues.quote: methodological variations among the studies... and heterogeniety of the host institution population led us to use a random- rather than fixed-effects model
